one_liner: Header-only AVX2 bilinear and nearest-neighbour resize for 8-bit grayscale; author claims 25-100% faster than OpenCV cv::resize.
what_it_does: KLERP<multithread>(src, src_w, src_h, dst, dst_w, dst_h) resizes a packed single-channel uint8 image with bilinear interpolation, and KNERP does nearest-neighbour with the same signature. It takes raw pointers and sizes (no row stride, no cv::Mat), so it replaces cv::resize(INTER_LINEAR or INTER_NEAREST) only for continuous CV_8UC1 buffers. Coordinate mapping (half-pixel centres, edge clamping) and 11-bit fixed-point weights are copied from OpenCV so the output is meant to match it.
how_it_is_fast: Separable fixed-point bilinear: per-call tables of source columns and 11-bit weights, a scalar horizontal pass into 32-bit row buffers, then an AVX2 vertical pass (shift right 4, packs, _mm256_mulhi_epi16 by the row weights, rounding shift, packus) that writes 32 pixels per iteration; this is the same arithmetic as OpenCV's VResizeLinearVec_32s8u. Horizontally filtered source rows are cached and reused when consecutive output rows map to the same source rows, which skips most of the horizontal work when upscaling. Outputs of 20000 pixels or more are split by rows across std::thread::hardware_concurrency() std::async tasks; KNERP is a scalar table-driven gather threaded the same way.
when_to_use: Upscaling 8-bit grayscale frames or ROIs on x86-64 with AVX2 where row reuse removes most of the horizontal pass.
Computer-vision code that already relies on OpenCV INTER_LINEAR fixed-point output but wants a dependency-free kernel for this one operation.
Single-threaded use (KLERP<false>), which avoids the threading defects below and is small enough (about 260 lines) to vendor and audit.
As a readable reference for OpenCV-compatible fixed-point bilinear resizing with AVX2.
when_not_to_use: Multithreaded calls on machines with many hardware threads unless the row split is patched: it writes past the end of dst for common heights (see gotchas).
Colour or multi-channel images, 16-bit or float data, or strided ROIs: only packed 8-bit single-channel buffers are supported.
CPUs without AVX2 or non-x86 targets: there is no SSE, NEON or scalar fallback for KLERP.
Area, bicubic or Lanczos filtering, or any case needing published, reproducible speed numbers: the repo has no OpenCV timing code.
Calling KLERP<true> or KNERP<true> from several threads at once: the calls share one function-static std::future array.

integration.form: header-only (KLERP.h), but its helper functions are not marked inline
integration.dependencies: none beyond the C++ standard library, <immintrin.h> and pthreads (Makefile links -lpthread)
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (Makefile uses g++ -std=gnu++14 -mavx2 -mfma -march=native -Ofast); compiler version not documented
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 (also uses the SSE4.1 _mm_round_ps); no other architectures
integration.thread_safety: KLERP<false> and KNERP<false> are reentrant; the <true> variants share a function-static array of std::future objects, so concurrent calls race
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: raw-pointer API for packed 8-bit single-channel images only; intended to reproduce cv::resize INTER_LINEAR / INTER_NEAREST output, but the repo never compares its output with OpenCV

gotchas: Heap overflow in the multithreaded row split (KLERP and KNERP): stride = ceil(dst_h / hardware_concurrency()) and hardware_concurrency()-1 full chunks are launched before the remainder, so whenever (threads-1)*stride > dst_h the tasks write rows past the end of dst (and read past the end of the weight table). A simulation of the split shows it for a 2000x10 output on 8 threads (4 extra rows), 1000x100 on 16 threads, and on 64 threads 1891 of the heights 2-4096, including 640x480 (15360 bytes past the buffer), 1280x720 and main.cpp's own 800x2000 (12800 bytes). Fix by launching only ceil(dst_h / stride) chunks.

_KNERP, pass1, pass2 and _KLERP are non-inline functions defined in the header, so including KLERP.h from two translation units gives duplicate-symbol link errors; add inline or include it in one .cpp.

Each multithreaded call starts its tasks with std::async(std::launch::async); libstdc++ and libc++ create a new thread per task (MSVC uses a pool), so outputs just above the 20000-pixel cutoff pay thread start-up on every call. A hardware_concurrency() of 0 would divide by zero.

The demo builds with -Ofast -mfma, which lets the compiler contract the double-precision coordinate maths into FMAs; bit-exact agreement with a given OpenCV build is plausible from the arithmetic but is not tested anywhere in the repo.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick KLERP only when a tiny dependency-free header for OpenCV-compatible bilinear on 8-bit grayscale matters more than evidence; CompV publishes measured speedups over cv::resize bilinear, and fast_image_resize, tir and stb-image-resize-opt cover multi-channel data and better filters with published benchmark tables.
verified_claims_summary: The only claim is the author's bare '25-100% faster than OpenCV' range with no per-case numbers, CPU, compiler, OpenCV version or thread settings; main.cpp times KLERP alone (2x2 input upscaled to 800x2000, multithreaded, 2000 runs) and never calls cv::resize. The code dates from December 2016, and OpenCV 4.x's resize.cpp still performs the same fixed-point vertical pass with universal intrinsics, so any lead now rests on row reuse and threading and has not been re-measured.
status_note: Abandoned: the code is a single 26 Dec 2016 commit and the only later commit (23 Mar 2021) added the MIT license; no issues or pull requests exist. Small enough to vendor, but patch the row split and mark the helpers inline first.
